The empty product $\epsilon_\emptyset$ and the signs $s(\emptyset,\{0,1,2,3\})$ and $s(\{0,1,2,3\},\emptyset)$ are $1$. For each increasing $I$, set $\star_\eta e^I=\epsilon_I s(I,I^c)e^{I^c}$. actual_current_step_excerpts.1.1: Put $s=x^2+y^2>0$, $P=-ys^{-1}$, and $Q=xs^{-1}$. Iterating the positive-base power rule in [F2] gives derivatives of every order of $u^{-1}$ on $u>0$; the chain and product rules therefore show that $P,Q$ are smooth on the punctured plane. Also by [F2], $\partial_xQ=s^{-1}-2x^2s^{-2}$ and $\partial_yP=-s^{-1}+2y^2s^{-2}$, so [F1] gives $dA=(2s^{-1}-2(x^2+y^2)s^{-2})\,dx\wedge dy=0$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]
actual_current_step_excerpts.1.2: By [F9], the coordinate functions of $\gamma(t)=(\cos(2\pi t),\sin(2\pi t))$ are smooth on all of $\mathbb R$, using composition with the affine function $2\pi t$ and the chain rule in [F2]. By [F10], $\cos^2(2\pi t)+\sin^2(2\pi t)=1$, so this extension takes values in the punctured plane. It therefore supplies the neighbourhood-smooth extension required for a singular one-simplex in [F3]. The zero values in [F10] and periodicity in [F11] give $\gamma(0)=\gamma(1)=(1,0)$, hence $\partial\gamma=0$. Differentiating by [F10] and the chain rule gives $\gamma^*dx=-2\pi\sin(2\pi t)\,dt$ and $\gamma^*dy=2\pi\cos(2\pi t)\,dt$. Thus the pulled-back numerator is $2\pi(\sin^2(2\pi t)+\cos^2(2\pi t))\,dt=2\pi\,dt$, and its denominator is $1$, so $\gamma^*A=2\pi\,dt$. In the positive affine coordinate on the standard one-simplex, [F5] and [F12] reduce its integral to the rectangle integral of the constant $2\pi$ on $[0,1]$. For any partition $0=t_0<\cdots<t_m=1$, every subinterval has infimum and supremum $2\pi$, so both Darboux sums equal $\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}2\pi(t_{i+1}-t_i)=2\pi$. Their lower supremum and upper infimum therefore agree at $2\pi$, proving $\int_\gamma A=2\pi>0$ by [F11]; [F4] identifies this as the period. If a globally defined smooth $\chi$ satisfied $A=d\chi$, then [F6] would give $\int_\gamma A=\int_\gamma d\chi=\int_{\partial\gamma}\chi=0$, contradicting that positive value. Thus $A$ is not globally exact. [F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F9, F10, F11, F12, given, algebra]

actual_current_step_excerpts.1.1: Let $A,B,C\in\{0,1\}$ be base indices and $i,j,k\in\{2,3\}$ sphere indices. In base coordinates, write $r_A:=\partial_A r$ and $r^A:=q^{AB}r_B$, the components of the vector field $q^{AB}\partial_Br$ (the $q$-dual of $dr$). The inverse metric is $g^{AB}=q^{AB}$ and $g^{ij}=r^{-2}\gamma^{ij}$. Substituting the block metric $g_{AB}=q_{AB}$, $g_{ij}=r^2\gamma_{ij}$, $g_{Ai}=0$ into [F4] gives the mixed Christoffels $\Gamma^A{}_{ij}=-\frac12q^{AB}\partial_B(r^2\gamma_{ij})=-r r^A\gamma_{ij}$ and $\Gamma^i{}_{Aj}=\frac12r^{-2}\gamma^{ik}\partial_A(r^2\gamma_{kj})=r^{-1}r_A\delta^i_j$. All other mixed Christoffels vanish because the inverse metric is block diagonal, $q_{AB}$ is independent of sphere coordinates, and $\gamma_{ij}$ is independent of base coordinates. The unit round sphere has $\Gamma^\theta{}_{\phi\phi}=-\sin\theta\cos\theta$ and $\Gamma^\phi{}_{\theta\phi}=\Gamma^\phi{}_{\phi\theta}=\cot\theta$ on the polar chart of [F6]. Substitution in [F5] and contraction by [F3] give $\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma)_{\theta\theta} =-\partial_\theta\cot\theta-\cot^2\theta=1$ and $\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma)_{\phi\phi} =\partial_\theta(-\sin\theta\cos\theta)-\cos^2\theta+2\cos^2\theta =\sin^2\theta$, with mixed component zero. Thus $\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma)=\gamma$ on that chart and everywhere by smoothness. [F1, F3, F4, F5, F6, given, algebra]

By [F2] there is a unique $[t]\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ for which $z=\cos(2\pi t)+i\sin(2\pi t)$. Put $\theta:=2\pi t$ modulo $2\pi$. If $n<0$, then [F3] gives $z\overline z=|z|^2=1$ because $z\in U(1)$, so $z^{-1}=\overline z$; by [F5], this is $\cos(-\theta)+i\sin(-\theta)$. Applying the same addition-formula induction to $z^{-1}$ proves the displayed formula for negative $n$. This proves the full character classification and the displayed formula. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, algebra]

actual_current_step_excerpts.1.1: Direct multiplication gives $\sigma_j^2=I$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_j)=0$, $\sigma_x\sigma_y=i\sigma_z$, $\sigma_y\sigma_z=i\sigma_x$, and $\sigma_z\sigma_x=i\sigma_y$; reversing the order negates each mixed product. Thus $\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_j\sigma_k)=2\delta_{jk}$. Since a Hermitian $2\times2$ matrix has two real diagonal entries and one complex off-diagonal entry, $\dim_{\mathbb R}\mathsf H_2=4$; the four nonzero orthogonal matrices $I,\sigma_x,\sigma_y,\sigma_z$ form a basis. Write $\rho=aI+\sum_jb_j\sigma_j$ in this basis. Since $\operatorname{Tr}(I)=2$ and $\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_j)=0$, the trace-one condition gives $a=1/2$; pairing with $\sigma_k$ gives $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\sigma_k)=2b_k$. Thus the representation is unique with $r_k:=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\sigma_k)=2b_k\in\mathbb R$. Write $r=(r_x,r_y,r_z)\in\mathbb R^3$ and $\|r\|_2=(r_x^2+r_y^2+r_z^2)^{1/2}$. Positivity [A2] restricts $\|r\|_2\le1$, since $(r_x\sigma_x+r_y\sigma_y+r_z\sigma_z)^2=\|r\|_2^2I$ and the eigenvalues of $\rho$ are $(1\pm\|r\|_2)/2$. [A1, A2, algebra]
